sections.text: O King! The more I think of that marvellous and holy discourse, the more I lose myself in joy.
As memory recalls again and again the exceeding beauty of the Lord, I am filled with amazement and happiness.
यत्र योगेश्वरः कृष्णो यत्र पार्थो धनुर्धरः।
Wherever is the Lord Shri Krishna, the Prince of Wisdom, and wherever is Arjuna, the Great Archer, I am more than convinced that good fortune, victory, happiness and righteousness will follow.

So we had been discussing chapter 18, Moksa Sannyas Yoga. We have come to the final concluding portion where Bhagavan has concluded his portion. Arjuna has confirmed that he is now completely in control of himself. His delusion is gone. He regained his memory. In other words, what is right and what is wrong, what needs to be done and whats to be avoided and what his real self is.
Im now ready to do whatever you have asked me to do. In other words, Im now ready to follow your instruction in Bhagavad Gita, which I have learnt so far from you. So I will now fight this war. Basically, when we are deluded and somebody gives advice and we are now ready to face the challenges of life, then we say, dont worry, Im now ready. I will fight this battle. Thats where Arjuna is now.
And the only other two people who are participating in this was Sanjaya, sitting in Dhritarashtras palace. Dhritarashtra, the blind king, who is somewhat a cause for this conflict. Had he done what needed to be done for him as a king, we wouldnt have the situation of these two armies facing each other. Because of his blindness, his ignorance about what is right and wrong, the situation led to this battle of the war. So hes sitting in his palace. Sanjay, his charioteer or the personal assistant, had narrated what was going on between the Krishna and Arjuna.
As we had discussed before, this was only possible because Bhagavan Ved Vyas, in his last-ditch effort to stop this war, goes to Dhritarashtra and says, You need to stop this. For you to see whats happening, I can give you a divine vision. This will lead to a disaster for the Kauravas. But Dhritarashtra was not comfortable, so he said, I do not want this vision. Give it to my secretary; he can narrate it to me. And thats how Sanjaya got the divine vision, so he could see everything while sitting in the palace.
For all practical purposes, Sanjaya became the first telecaster who narrated what was happening in a distant place. He was given this vision so that he could not only see what was happening there, but also hear what Krishna and Arjuna were talking about, and even see in their minds what they were thinking. So now, since Arjuna has concluded, Sanjaya gives the final comments. The last five verses are Sanjayas -- he is the third party. Arjuna was involved in it completely.
He was the recipient of this knowledge. Knowledge was directly given to him. Krishna was the giver of the knowledge, and he obviously had not only Arjuna but everyones betterment in mind. Sanjaya is the third party, looking at the situation, and now gives his version of what he has seen.
So the next five verses which conclude Bhagavad Gita -- Sanjaya said: Ithi Aham Vasudevashya Parthasyacha Mahatmanah Samvadam Imam Ashrausham Adbhutam Romaharshanam. He said, This is me witnessing the dialogue between Vasudeva and Partha. Krishna is called Vasudeva because he is the son of Vasudeva -- Vasudevasutam Devam, Devakis son. Hes also called Vasudeva because he is the Deva of the Vasavas.
The Vasavas, as we learned in chapter 10, are the deities of the seasons. There are eight seasons, and each season has its own presiding deity. As we have said, in our culture everything is personified, and nothing can really work in a chaotic situation. Everything has its own order. If there is order, we absolutely know there is a controller -- without any laws or enforcing agency, there cannot be any order. Since in nature there is a perfect order, there have to be lawmakers and law enforcers. The enforcing deities for these seasons are the Vasavas, the Vasus.
These eight Vasus are controlling the eight seasons. As we may have discussed before, the six seasons we commonly know are summer, winter, monsoon, and then subsets like spring and fall -- so there are six seasons. Where are the other two? The other two are in our mind: happiness and unhappiness.
So two micro seasons and six macro seasons make eight, with their presiding deities. All Vasus are Vasavas, and the Deva of the Vasus is Vasudeva. So he is the Deva of all the seasons -- in other words, the Deva of all the seasons in our life. He is the presiding deity, Vasudeva, the consciousness. All these eight seasons are perceived by me because consciousness is functioning through me.
So this is the dialogue between Vasudeva and Mahatmana Partha -- High-Souled Arjuna. Arjuna is called High-Souled here not because he was Krishnas cousin or Pandus son, but because he is a normal man who faced the challenges of life and broke down -- yet he had the courage to listen to the right advice and rise to the situation. Therefore he is high-souled: not because he was perfect, not because he had no faults, but because he had the normal faults of a normal person and the courage to overcome them. So Sanjaya said, The dialogue between the supreme self, the sacred, and the normal man Partha -- listening to this, I am so thrilled that I am having goosebumps.
What have I experienced so wonderful? He said this was an incredible dialogue which he never thought he would be able to witness in his life. And then he continues: Vyasa Prasadat Shrutavan Etat Guhyam Aham Param Yogam Yogeshwarat Krishnat Sakshat Kathayatah Svayam. I had the good fortune of listening to this dialogue because of Vyasa Prasadat. I was not capable of listening to it on my own. I would never have been able to see what Krishna and Arjuna were talking about. It was possible for me to hear because of the grace of Vyasa. We have seen why Vyasa gave him the divine vision, and therefore he could listen to it.
Any experience which I feel is incredible in my life, I always think it came to me by somebodys grace -- in this case, Vyasas grace. He said, Yogam Yogeshwarat Krishnat Sakshat Kathayatah -- this dialogue which describes the yoga, I heard directly from the mouth of Yogeshwara Krishna. We have learned before that Krishna is Yogeshwara -- he is the Lord of Yoga, the perfect Avatara. There was never a time he was not connected with his supreme self. He was always a man walking on this earth, yet always connected with his supreme self. One who is connected with his supreme self is a Yogi.
Krishna is Yogeshwara. He is the Lord of all yogis, because there was never a time in his life, from the time he was born till he left, when he was not connected to his supreme self. Sanjaya says, I heard from a person who is Yogeshwara, from his mouth directly. In other words, its not that this was something completely new to him.
Growing up in Vedic culture as the minister or private secretary of the great king, he had heard these things before. But now he heard directly from the Lord himself, the one who is one with the supreme self. So this now completely clarifies any doubt he ever had in his mind. This is now his direct knowledge. He experienced directly what the Lord has said. The next verse says: Rajan Samsmritya Samsmritya Samvadam Imam Adbhutam Keshava Arjunayoho Punyam Hrishyami Cha Muhurmuhuhu.
I keep remembering what I have just experienced, over and over again. The more I think about it, the more joy it gives me -- to know that the self is immutable, imperishable. More and more I remember, and it gives me great strength and great joy, that I have heard from the great soul what reality is. So Sanjaya is trying to impress upon Dhritarashtra: you are not facing somebody mortal -- your sons are facing someone who is the Lord himself, who has direct knowledge. And he will be on Arjunas side.
Tat Cha Samsmritya Samsmritya Rupam Atyadbhutam Hareho Vismayo Me Mahan Rajan Hrishyami Cha Punaha Punaha. Not only did I hear the dialogue between the two, but I also saw his Virat Rupa, his cosmic form. Ive seen your sons going into his mouth and getting crushed. I have seen these Mahatmas praising him, some in fear and some in awe. That wondrous vision -- Tat Samsmritya Hareho -- that wonderful, magnificent form, he keeps remembering over and over again. And he is wonderstruck.
I am completely wonderstruck about that vision. O Rajan, Hrishyami Cha Punaha Punaha. I rejoice again and again just remembering the Lords complete form. And I know that the victory will be on the side of the truth. Obviously all the good people who knew what is right, including Drona, Bheeshma, Sanjaya, Vidur. But they could not be on the Pandava side because of the Niti Shastra at that time, if you have eaten somebodys salt, in other words, if youre obliged by somebody, you have to be on their side, no matter how wrong he is.
Therefore they cannot be on the Pandavas side. But they are making every effort to see whether Dhritarashtra changes his mind. He is the one person who has complete control to stop this war right then and there. But as we have said, he has already confessed he is very comfortable in his blindness, in his ignorance. He does not want to come out of his comfort zone of what he knows. This is basically where we are at some level -- clinging to something familiar.
We are afraid of change. Thats why from one generation to another there is always a generation gap. In my old age, I am so comfortable in what I do. I get completely baffled by all this technology and social media. And so we need support from somebody younger who can guide us.
Thats a source of wonder for me. The last verse is the complete conclusion of what Sanjaya has learned. But this is not merely Sanjayas opinion -- it is a direct teaching for us on how to live life. It says: Yatra Yogeshwara Krishna Yatra Partha Dhanurdharaha Tatra Shri Vijaya Bhutihi Dhruvah Nitihi Matir Mama. Where there is Yogeshwara Krishna -- he didnt simply say just Krishna.
Where there is Krishna, where there is Arjuna -- Yatra Yogeshwara Krishna -- where there is the Lord of Yoga, the Lord Krishna. And what does that mean for us? That person is the one who is always one with his supreme self. That Yogeshwara Krishna is present in our consciousness. When we invoke our consciousness, our divine vision -- the sacred in us, the divine in us -- along with Yatra Partha Dhanurdharaha, where there is Arjuna with his bow and arrow ready to fight -- not lying on the ground as was the case in the first chapter. When we face challenges in this life, we have the tools to fight this battle.
But we get dejected and put our tools down and say Im not ready. So we cannot win that battle and therefore there cannot be any success. World will be what it is. You will be facing this battle of life no matter how sacred and pious you are. Because thats the nature of the world. What you have to be is Dhanurdhara Partha -- not just Partha, but Dhanurdhara Partha. Partha is a common man like you and I.
The only difference is hes ready to fight. So when you are ready to fight the challenges of life -- but not just with your ego saying, I can take care of myself --

The Gita concludes with Sanjayas joyful declaration. Verses 76-77: repeatedly remembering this wonderful, sacred dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna, I rejoice again and again. Recalling that supremely wondrous form of Hari, great is my amazement, and I rejoice repeatedly. The teaching has not just informed Sanjaya but transformed him. He cannot stop thinking about it, and each remembrance brings fresh joy and wonder.
Verse 78 is the Gitas triumphant conclusion: yatra Yogeshvara Krishna yatra Partho dhanurdharah tatra shrir vijayo bhutir dhruva nitir - wherever is Krishna, the Lord of Yoga, and Arjuna, the archer with bow ready, there are fortune, victory, prosperity, and firm righteousness. This is the promise and the formula. When higher wisdom (Krishna/Yogeshvara) combines with prepared, committed action (Arjuna/Dhanurdhara), success is assured.
This final verse is your daily practice in condensed form: Invoke the Lord of Yoga in your heart - the wisdom, the guidance, the connection to the Supreme. Then take up your bow - bring your skills, your preparation, your readiness to act. Together, these ensure victory - not necessarily the victory your ego envisions, but the victory of dharma, the triumph of what is right. Today, bring both elements to whatever challenge you face: yogeshvara (higher guidance) and dhanurdhara (capable readiness). Neither alone is sufficient - passive wisdom without action, or frantic action without wisdom, both fail. United, they are invincible. This is the Gitas final teaching: connect to the Source, prepare yourself, act decisively. Shri, vijaya, bhuti, and dhruva niti will follow.
